The best advice I can give you is to become your own advocate. I am current fighting a brain tumor and I have had to call, write, and refuse to leave a doctor's office just to get treatment. Your doctors are probably hard working people but they are not infallible. Don't take their word for something just because they said it authoritatively. Research, research, research. Wikipedia is surprisingly helpful at breaking down complex subjects in a way that you can understand them. Don't be afraid to get a second opinion. If your doctor has a problem with you consulting other physicians about your treatment then he is not a good doctor.

Get a binder and keep all of your health information in it. I suggest making the first page a timeline that shows any relevant or abnormal tests. It should include date, test, result, any treatment given to correct the abnormal results. That will really help any doctor you visit. Instead of wading through a mess of paperwork they will have a nice summary to help them see patterns in your test results. The next page should be a table of contents so that your doctor can easily find results from a test. My binder is divided into several sections: Blood work/lab results, imaging studies, hospitalizations, non-hospitalization physician's notes( which is further divided by specialty cardiology, oncology, etc), medications, and the last section is symptoms I have organized by date of onset with notes on how they progressed over time. You are not your doctor's only patient. If you make his job easier by organizing information for him he will appreciate it and be able to give you better care.

Oh yeah I got a pretty extensive history of dealing complex medical services (born with spina bifida) along with bureaucracy (did six years in the military so I've dealt with the VA healthcare system). Being organized is critical and I didn't even think about it until you mentioned it.
